items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌙 The most famous line in the speech nearly went unheard. Right before it, Kennedy landed a joke about a football rivalry that got such a big laugh from the crowd that the iconic words almost got buried under it. "We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard."

On September 12, 1962, President John F. Kennedy stood before around 40,000 people in the sweltering heat of Rice Stadium in Houston, Texas, and made the case for sending Americans to the Moon. At the time, this was an almost outrageous promise. The United States had barely managed to put a man in orbit. The technology to reach the Moon did not exist yet.

What makes the speech remarkable is how honestly it faced that gap. Kennedy wasn't promising something easy. He was asking the country to commit to something genuinely hard, with no guarantee it would work, and to fund it, and to see it through.

A May 1961 poll had shown only 42 percent of Americans backed the idea. The speech was meant to change that. Seven years later, Apollo 11 landed. After Neil Armstrong stepped onto the surface, someone left flowers at Kennedy's grave with a note: "Mr. President, the Eagle has landed."

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌊 Saturn’s icy moon Enceladus now has the full chemical toolkit for life as we know it.

Scientists have confirmed phosphorus in tiny ice grains blasted from Enceladus’s hidden ocean into space.

That matters because phosphorus was the last major missing element in the famous CHNOPS list: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur.

Together, these six elements are essential to life on Earth.

They help build DNA, RNA, proteins, cell membranes and the energy-carrying molecules that keep living cells running.

Enceladus already had a strong case for habitability.

NASA’s Cassini spacecraft found that the moon has a global ocean beneath its icy shell, organic compounds in its plume, salts, and signs of hydrothermal chemistry on the ocean floor.

Now, the detection of sodium phosphates in ocean-derived ice grains makes the case even stronger.

The study also suggests that phosphate may be at least 100 times more concentrated in Enceladus’s plume-forming ocean waters than in Earth’s oceans.

This does not mean life has been found.

But it means Enceladus has liquid water, possible energy sources and the major chemical ingredients life needs.

A tiny moon around Saturn has become one of the most promising places to search for life beyond Earth.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Postberg et al., “Detection of phosphates originating from Enceladus’s ocean”, Nature (2023)

On the evening of September 14, a slender waxing crescent Moon shines close to brilliant Venus, low in the west-southwest, with Spica glinting nearby in Virgo. 

Venus is near its greatest brilliancy for the year, blazing around magnitude -4.7 and utterly unmistakable even in bright twilight. Spica, fainter and blue-white, sits close by, while the Moon's dark side glows softly with earthshine, sunlight reflected off Earth.

🔭 The trio hangs low near the horizon, so find a clear, unobstructed western view and look about 30 to 45 minutes after sunset. From parts of the world, the Moon actually passes in front of Venus in an occultation; elsewhere it's simply a beautiful close pairing. Binoculars frame all three nicely. Catch it soon after sunset, as they set within about an hour 🌙✨

🌊 Saturn’s “Death Star” moon may be hiding one of the youngest oceans in the Solar System.

The moon is Mimas, a small icy world only about 400 kilometers wide.

At first glance, Mimas looks almost dead. Its surface is heavily cratered, and its giant Herschel crater makes it look like the Death Star from Star Wars.

That is why this discovery surprised scientists.

Using data from NASA’s Cassini spacecraft, researchers studied tiny changes in Mimas’s orbit around Saturn.

Those changes are hard to explain if Mimas is frozen solid all the way through.

The best fit is a global ocean of liquid water beneath an icy shell about 20 to 30 kilometers thick.

Even stranger, the ocean appears to be extremely young.

Models suggest it may have formed only 5 to 15 million years ago, possibly because Saturn’s tides recently began heating Mimas’s interior.

That may explain why the surface still looks old and quiet.

The ocean has not existed long enough to crack the crust or produce Enceladus-like geysers.

Mimas was one of the last places scientists expected to find liquid water.

Now, it may be a hidden ocean world caught near the beginning of its life.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Lainey et al., “A recently formed ocean inside Saturn’s moon Mimas”, Nature (2024)

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌕 Venus may have once had a moon, and then destroyed it.

Today, Venus has no natural satellite. That has always been strange, because Venus is so similar to Earth in size, mass and rocky composition.

Earth has a large Moon.

Venus has nothing.

A new study tested whether Venus could have formed a moon after a giant impact, only to lose it later through tides.

The team modeled a gravitational tug-of-war between Venus, the Sun and a hypothetical moon over billions of years.

The result was surprisingly brutal.

In many scenarios, the moon first moved outward, much like our Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth today.

But as the moon drained Venus’ spin, the balance changed.

Its orbit could reverse, forcing the moon to spiral back inward toward the planet.

Once it crossed Venus’ Roche limit, the moon would be torn apart by gravity, briefly forming a ring before much of the debris rained down onto Venus.

A heavier moon would not necessarily survive longer.

It could actually speed up its own destruction by slowing Venus faster.

This does not prove Venus had a moon.

But it shows that if it did, Venus may have swallowed the evidence long ago.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Kane et al., “Tidal Demise: The Evolution and Fate of a Hypothetical Venus Moon”, The Astrophysical Journal, accepted (2026)

ELEPHANT IN THE ROOM: I recently posted a sunset image over Lake Ontario/America. Perhaps not surprisingly, that generated a barrage of thoughts and opinions surrounding my referencing both Ontario & America. I understand there are some heated opinions on this topic. I'm hoping this post helps you understand the logic of why I'm referencing both. 

First and foremost, this page doesn't play politics. I certainly have my own personal opinions on the topic but they're not relevant here. As a government entity, the National Weather Service will be transitioning over to referencing Lake America. That means you'll be seeing the name change reflected in their forecast messaging. I don't have to like it or agree with it, but that is a fact. While I am under no similar obligation, my role as a meteorologist demands clarity. Picking one name over the other introduces room for a lack of clarity in messaging, particularly when we serve as a liaison to headlines they issue. That doesn't help anyone.

items.author: TornadoChasing
items.text:
Being my 19th birthday, I decided to skip my college classes for the day. My dad had called me that morning and told me about the first plane. 

At the time, we had no idea it was an attack and sort of joked "how does some idiot crash into a building that large." We didn't know it was a full size jet. We thought it was a small personal plane.

Turned on the TV to check the news just as plane two hit....the room went silent. This was no longer an accident...and the entire demeanor changed. 

Dad called me back and said "I think you should stay home from school." (lol he didn't know his degenerate son already planned to skip it.)

One by one, all the other TV stations stopped their programing for the day. Something unheard of back in the day. Remember, this is pre-everything about the modern internet era. No fb, no X, no YT, no phone apps, NONE of the crap we all use today. Just AIM, land lines and clunky Nokia cell phones with a snake game when text messages cost 10 cents each.

From there on, 24/7 news coverage. Staring at the TV. My family attempted a sad Bday dinner at a local restaurant but it was nothing but silence staring at the TV letting the food get cold. 

The day just got worse and worse as it evolved. The Pentagon, UA flight 93 and the heroes who forced the plane to not reach its likely target (the white house.)

Living next to Midway Airport in Chicago, and used to the noisy traffic of planes constantly taking off and landing, an eery silence fell over the hood once the FAA grounded all flights. It was unnatural, it was creepy. 

Until the fighter jets showed up. Is this really happening??

Everything changed that day. Terrorism was sort of just a bla bla thing we knew existed but still felt immune to. That day it became really real. We never felt more vulnerable.

Then, in the days after, we were never more united. It sucks it takes something like that to bring unity....but the unity was beautiful. Something I wish would happen again (minus the tragedy obviously) but probably never will.

Those too young to remember or born after will never understand such a level of unity, nor how the world changed. I wish they could experience what real unity feels like, and hope they never have to live through a day like that.  

For those who lived it, Never Forget. For those who didn't, try to understand.

TIMES ARE CHANGING: We all know the days are getting shorter this time of year. But it's so much deeper than that. 

The path our Sun takes in the sky is dramatically changing. On the summer solstice, the Sun climbs as high as 70° in the sky, eventually setting in on the northwest horizon. Today, the peak angle is only 51° with the Sun setting closer to due west. When winter arrives, the Sun rises only 23° and sets very early in the west-southwestern sky. This is the byproduct of Earth's axial tilt. Pay attention the next time your watch a sunset. Make a mental note of where on the horizon it sets. You'll notice it slowly changing locations each evening!

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
💨 Webb has caught a giant planet leaking helium into space.

The planet is WASP-107b, a strange super-puff world about 212 light-years away in the constellation Virgo.

It is almost the size of Jupiter, but has only about 12% of Jupiter’s mass.

That makes it so low-density that astronomers often compare it to cotton candy.

Using JWST’s NIRISS instrument, scientists watched starlight pass through the planet’s extended atmosphere.

They found helium absorption beginning about 1.5 hours before the planet even started crossing its star.

That means the gas is not just sitting close to the planet.

It is streaming far into space.

Models show helium flowing both ahead of and behind WASP-107b, forming long tails that stretch up to nearly 10 times the planet’s radius.

The planet orbits extremely close to its star, where radiation and stellar wind can strip away its outer atmosphere.

Webb also confirmed water in the atmosphere and found signs of strong chemical mixing.

Together, the results suggest WASP-107b may have formed farther out, then migrated inward, where its atmosphere became inflated and began escaping.

This is not just a planet with a leaky sky.

It is a world being reshaped by its star in real time.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Krishnamurthy et al., “Continuous helium absorption from both the leading and trailing tails of WASP-107 b”, Nature Astronomy (2026)

🌗 Astronomers have found a dead star with two completely different faces.

The object is a white dwarf called ZTF J203349.8+322901.1, about 1,300 light-years away in Cygnus.

White dwarfs are the dense leftover cores of stars like the Sun. They pack roughly a star’s worth of mass into a body about the size of Earth.

But this one is unlike any white dwarf seen before.

As it spins once every 15 minutes, its spectrum changes dramatically.

When one side faces Earth, astronomers see hydrogen. When the other side rotates into view, they see helium.

That is why the team nicknamed it Janus, after the two-faced Roman god of transition.

The star is probably caught during a rare phase in white dwarf evolution, when its outer atmosphere is changing from hydrogen-dominated to helium-dominated as it cools.

Normally, this transition should happen across the whole star.

But Janus seems split in half.

The leading idea is that a weak magnetic field may be controlling how material mixes across its surface, allowing helium to rise on one side while hydrogen remains on the other.

It is a strange glimpse of a dying star mid-transformation.

A cosmic corpse with two faces, turning every 15 minutes.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Caiazzo et al., “A rotating white dwarf shows different compositions on its opposite faces”, Nature (2023)

SEPT 11, 2001 | The satellite image of the U.S. Northeast Coast is one for the history books on Sept. 11, 2001. 

While New York City was in a state of emergency & the rest of the world was trying to come to grips with what happened, a massive hurricane was just offshore: Erin. 

On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, Erin was large, with a giant eye. Winds were 90 mph & the hurricane was beginning to turn toward the northeast, away from the U.S.

The reason for the turn? A cold front had moved through the Northeast the day before. North winds behind the front brought drier, more comfortable conditions. It also cleared out the sky, giving New York those deep blue skies seen in all videos from that day. 

North winds behind the front pushed the smoke from the Twin Towers south. The smoke was so pronounced that when zooming in to the NASA satellite image of Erin below, you can actually see it moving south into New York Harbor & New Jersey.   

A weather image that will forever be part of American history.

🔋 Aging may dim the cell’s power grid — and scientists may have found one reason why.

Mitochondria, the tiny structures that help cells produce energy, become less flexible and efficient with age.

A new study points to a molecule called phosphatidylcholine, a major fat-like building block of cell and mitochondrial membranes.

Researchers found that phosphatidylcholine production declines with age in worms, human cells, and human biological data.

As levels dropped, mitochondria became more fragmented and less able to adapt to energy demands.

But when older worms were given phosphatidylcholine or choline, a nutrient the body can use to make it, their mitochondria regained a more youthful structure and function.

This is promising, but not proof that supplements reverse aging in humans.

The real discovery is more careful: some cellular aging processes may be more flexible than we once thought.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Poliezhaieva et al., “Aging-associated decline of phosphatidylcholine synthesis is a malleable trigger of natural mitochondrial aging”, Nature Communications (2026)

WHERE WERE YOU 25 YEARS AGO TODAY?
🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸🇺🇸

On September 11, 2001, I was on a flight from Myrtle Beach to Charlotte when the Twin Towers were struck. I had no idea what had happened until I stepped off the plane and saw crowds gathered around TVs in silence. As we all watched in shock, word came that another plane had hit the Pentagon. A chill went through me, and the sound of a collective gasp filled the concourse.

No one felt safe. Many were terrified that Charlotte’s airport could be next, and honestly, it didn’t feel impossible. My final destination didn’t matter anymore…the skies were shut down. Later that morning, I walked out of one of the nation’s busiest airports into an eerie quiet, no jet engines, no takeoffs, no landings. Just silence.

Like millions of others, I spent the rest of the day glued to the television, watching in disbelief. I had never experienced anything like it, and I hope we never do again.

Twenty-five years later, I still pray for every life lost that day and for the families who continue to grieve. I also think of the thousands who have given their lives since then defending our freedom, and I pray for them and their families too.

9/11 was a moment when America came together, united in sorrow and patriotism. I wish we still held that same closeness today.

🇺🇸#NeverForget 🇺🇸

🫖 Tea may give aging bones a small boost, while too much coffee may do the opposite.

Researchers followed 9,704 women aged 65 and older for about 10 years, repeatedly tracking coffee and tea intake alongside bone mineral density at the hip and femoral neck.

Tea drinkers had slightly higher total hip bone density than non-tea drinkers. The difference was small, but statistically significant.

Coffee told a more cautious story. Moderate intake, around two to three cups per day, was not clearly harmful. But drinking more than five cups daily was linked to lower bone density.

The effect also seemed stronger in women with higher lifetime alcohol intake.

This does not prove coffee weakens bones or tea protects them. The study was observational.

But it suggests that for older women, what is in the cup may play a small role in long-term bone health.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Liu and Liu, “Longitudinal Association of Coffee and Tea Consumption with Bone Mineral Density in Older Women: A 10-Year Repeated-Measures Analysis in the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures”, Nutrients (2025)

PNW SATURDAY STORMS⛈️a compact upper-level low will move inland across southwestern Washington and northwestern Oregon Saturday, bringing widespread showers and unusually cold air aloft. As the colder air moves over the relatively milder surface, temperatures will decrease rapidly with height, creating steeper lapse rates and increasing atmospheric instability. This setup can support scattered thunderstorms capable of lightning, brief heavy rain, gusty winds and small hail.

The circulation around the low will also increase localized low-level wind shear and spin in the atmosphere. Convergence boundaries beneath the low could concentrate that rotation, allowing stronger shower updrafts to stretch it vertically and produce cold-air funnel clouds. Most cold-air funnels remain weak and never reach the ground, but an isolated brief touchdown cannot be ruled out, especially near the coast or over the open waters of the Pacific.

If you have outdoor plans, such as hiking, camping or boating, be prepared for storms and move indoors and off water quickly if storms approach⛈️

⚠️ A common pregnancy painkiller is raising new questions — but the evidence needs caution.

Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, is widely used during pregnancy because many other painkillers are considered riskier.

In the Danish COPANA cohort, researchers followed pregnant women and examined their infants around three months of age.

Among 302 girls, prenatal paracetamol exposure was linked with smaller average ovarian volume, fewer ovarian follicles, smaller uterine volume, and lower reproductive-hormone markers.

A related analysis in 287 boys also reported smaller average testis volume after early fetal exposure.

But this was observational. It cannot prove paracetamol caused the differences, and it does not show these children will have fertility problems later.

Experts say current advice should not change suddenly. Untreated fever and severe pain in pregnancy can also carry risks.

The safest message is simple: use paracetamol only when needed, at the lowest effective dose, and with medical guidance during pregnancy.

📃 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Fischer et al., “Fetal exposure to paracetamol is associated with altered markers of ovarian development and reduced uterine volume in girls: the COPANA study”, Human Reproduction Open (2026)

items.text:
🧬 Scientists have found life-related sugars inside samples from asteroid Bennu.

The samples were collected by NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission, which touched asteroid Bennu in 2020 and returned its material safely to Earth in 2023.

Now, researchers have found several bio-essential sugars inside that pristine asteroid dust.

The most important one is ribose, the sugar used to build RNA.

That matters because RNA is central to one major origin-of-life idea called the RNA world, where early life may have relied on RNA before DNA became the main genetic storage molecule.

The Bennu sample also contained glucose, one of the most common energy sources used by life on Earth.

This does not mean Bennu was alive.

It means the chemistry needed for life was already happening inside ancient asteroid material formed more than 4.5 billion years ago.

The discovery builds on earlier Bennu findings of amino acids, phosphate, ammonia and all five nucleobases used by DNA and RNA.

Together, these results are making one idea harder to ignore.

Asteroids may have helped deliver the raw molecular toolkit from which life on Earth began.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Furukawa et al., “Bio-essential sugars in samples from asteroid Bennu”, Nature Geoscience (2025)

The catch this year is that we have nothing active, and nothing is expected to develop over the next 7 days. With no season in the satellite era having failed to produce a hurricane by September 11th, this season is now approaching unprecedented territory.

While there is still plenty of time left in the season, the lack of activity heading into the climatological peak even for El Nino standards is rather shocking. It remains to be seen whether things will finally ramp up later in September and October.

GUSTY WINDS TODAY | FIRE & BLOWING DUST RISK🌬️🔥💨a dry cold front moving across the Inland Northwest today will bring a noticeable increase in west to northwest winds, especially this afternoon and evening!

The strongest winds are expected through the Cascade gaps, Kittitas Valley, Columbia Gorge, Wenatchee area, Waterville Plateau and parts of the Columbia Basin, where sustained winds of 20-25 mph with gusts around 30-40+ mph are possible. Farther east, including around Moses Lake, Spokane, the Palouse and Lewiston-Pullman, gusts will generally reach 20-30 mph. Winds should peak roughly 1-5PM before gradually relaxing.

The wind will combine with dry vegetation and lower humidity, creating elevated fire weather conditions. Humidity could fall into the teens to lower 20s in some areas. Any existing fires could spread more rapidly, and new fires could become difficult to control during the strongest winds.

There is also a localized blowing-dust risk across the Columbia Basin, particularly along I-90 from Moses Lake toward Ritzville and areas farther south. Visibility could suddenly fall to a mile or less in the most affected spots🌬️🔥💨

items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🌌 A dark matter detector nearly a mile underground has recorded a signal scientists cannot yet explain.

The signal came from LUX-ZEPLIN, or LZ, one of the world’s most sensitive dark matter experiments.

It sits deep beneath South Dakota inside the Sanford Underground Research Facility, shielded from cosmic rays by nearly a mile of rock.

At its heart are tonnes of ultra-pure liquid xenon, waiting for the faint flash that could be caused by a dark matter particle.

In a new analysis, researchers studied 220 live days of data collected between March 2023 and April 2024.

They found one event that looked like a nuclear recoil of about 248 keV.

That means something appears to have struck a xenon nucleus and made it recoil.

The strange part is that the event appeared in a region where ordinary background signals should be very rare.

If it was caused by dark matter, the particle may be a WIMP at least 200 times heavier than a proton.

But one event is not a discovery.

The signal currently stands at 2.6 sigma, meaning it could still be a rare background event.

For now, LZ has not found dark matter.

But it may have found its most interesting hint yet.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Akerib et al., “Search for dark matter particle interactions in an extended nuclear recoil energy window with the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment”, arXiv preprint, submitted to Physical Review Letters (2026)
